topics.title: Core Concepts
topics.description: The Kafka vocabulary. Topic, partition, offset and consumer group are what everything else is built on.

rows: Unit of parallelism and ordering. A topic is split into N partitions, and ordering is guaranteed only within a partition.
Position of a record in a partition; consumers track their own offsets
Writes records. A key routes the record to a partition via hash(key) % partitions, so the same key always lands on the same partition and stays ordered.
Set of consumers sharing the work; each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in the group
Kafka server. Partitions are replicated across brokers (leader plus followers, replication.factor=3 typical).
Events are kept for a time or size limit (for example 7 days) regardless of consumption, so consumers can replay

topics.title: Kafka vs Queues
topics.description: How Kafka differs from RabbitMQ, SQS and JMS, and how to justify picking one.
kafka: The log is retained, so events are replayable
Consumers pull and track their own offsets
Multiple independent groups read the same events
choosing: RabbitMQ for complex routing: header and topic exchanges, per-message TTL, priorities
Kafka for event streaming, audit, high volume, and multiple readers

topics.title: Delivery Semantics
topics.description: The number one Kafka interview topic. Know the three options and which one you actually design for.

rows: Duplicates on retry, so consumers must be idempotent
Kafka transactions plus an idempotent producer (enable.idempotence=true); practical within Kafka Streams pipelines
Complex, and it ends at external systems

topics.the_line_to_say: I design for at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers, deduping on a unique business key or a processed-events table. True exactly-once across arbitrary systems does not exist; idempotency is how you get its effect.
producer_acks: acks=1 waits for the leader only
acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 is durable. Say this one for money-related events.

topics.title: Consumer Groups
topics.description: Scaling consumers, what a rebalance costs you, and the one metric to alert on.

key_points.description: Scale consumers up to the partition count. Beyond that, the extra consumers sit idle.
Partitions are reassigned when members join or leave, causing a brief pause. Long processing plus missed heartbeats causes rebalance storms (max.poll.interval.ms).
Newest offset minus committed offset. This is the key health metric; alert on growing lag.
Retry N times, then send the record to a Dead Letter Topic with error metadata. Never block the partition forever.

topics.title: Spring Kafka
topics.description: A producer keyed for ordering, an idempotent consumer with manual acknowledgment, and the config that makes it at-least-once.

configuration.title: application.yml
configuration.code:
spring.kafka:
  consumer:
    enable-auto-commit: false     # manual ack = at-least-once
    auto-offset-reset: earliest
  listener:
    ack-mode: manual

topics.title: Outbox Pattern
topics.description: The transactional outbox, asked constantly alongside microservices.
topics.problem: Saving to the database and publishing to Kafka cannot be made atomic.
topics.solution: Write the event into an outbox table in the same database transaction as the business change. A relay, either Debezium CDC or a poller, then publishes it to Kafka. No lost events and no phantom events.

topics.title: Saga Pattern
topics.description: How distributed transactions actually get done across services.
topics.how_it_works: A sequence of local transactions coordinated by events. Failures trigger compensating actions such as issuing a refund or releasing stock.

approaches.name: Choreography
approaches.description: Services react to each other's events. Loosely coupled, but hard to follow end to end.

approaches.name: Orchestration
approaches.description: A central coordinator drives the flow, for example the order service or a state machine. Visible and traceable, but adds a coordinator.

topics.title: System Design
topics.description: How to bring Kafka into a system design answer.
points: Partition count is your maximum parallelism. Pick a key that distributes well but still preserves the ordering you need, such as user_id or order_id.
Hot partition problem: a celebrity key overloads one partition. Add a salt or bucket suffix and aggregate downstream.
Backpressure: consumers pull at their own pace, so spikes buffer in the log instead of killing services.
Retention as a feature: rebuild a new service's state by replaying from offset 0.

topics.title: Interview Q&A
topics.description: The five questions that come up most, with the answers to give.

questions.question: How does Kafka guarantee ordering?
questions.answer: Only within a partition. The same key goes to the same partition and is FIFO there. Global ordering requires a single partition, which caps throughput, so usually you restructure the problem so that per-key ordering suffices.

questions.question: What happens when a consumer crashes mid-processing?
questions.answer: Offsets stay uncommitted, so after the rebalance another consumer reprocesses from the last commit. That produces duplicates, which is exactly why consumers must be idempotent under at-least-once delivery.

questions.question: Kafka vs RabbitMQ, when each?
questions.answer: RabbitMQ for task queues, complex routing, per-message acknowledgment and priority, and lower latency at low volume. Kafka for event streaming, replay, multiple consumer groups, ordering per key, very high throughput, and audit or event sourcing.

questions.question: How do you avoid losing messages end-to-end?
questions.answer: Producer: acks=all, idempotent producer, retries. Broker: replication of at least 3 with min.insync.replicas=2. Consumer: commit after processing, a Dead Letter Topic for poison messages, and monitoring on lag. Plus the outbox pattern so the database and the topic never diverge.

questions.question: How would you migrate a synchronous REST call between services to events?
questions.answer: First establish that the caller does not need the response synchronously. Then publish a domain event through the outbox, have the consumer process it with retries, and expose a read model or callback for status. Keep the REST path during migration behind a feature flag.
